audits.claim: Script-origin hypotheses involve Iranian/Aramaic-derived writing traditions with debated routes, and a completely demonstrated Sogdian-to-Orkhon family tree is not assumed (flagged to-verify).
audits.retrieval_status: Retrieved full OA repository copy (real.mtak.hu, 14 PDF pages), converted with pdftotext and read locally.
audits.source_locator: A. Róna-Tas, 'On the Development and Origin of the East Turkic "Runic" Script', Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 41(1) 1987, 7-14; opening paragraph (p.7) and concluding summary (pp.11-12).
audits.source_excerpt: 'there is still uncertainty about its origin' ... 'Neither of the hitherto suggested hypothesises is convincing' ... 'The Turks took over a form of Aramaic alphabet, which stood near to, but was not identical with, Sogdian or Armazic.' (30 words)
audits.basis: The retrieved article states the origin remains uncertain, reports Clauson's (1970) Iranian-plus-Greek hypothesis and Livšic's (1978) all-Sogdian hypothesis, calls both unconvincing, and concludes an Aramaic-derived prototype near but not identical to Sogdian/Armazic. That is exactly the entry's claim that routes are debated and that no fully demonstrated Sogdian-to-Orkhon descent should be assumed. The (to-verify) flag stands as written; no erratum was appended because nothing checked here was contradicted.
audits.access_limit: None for this source (open repository PDF). A 1987 synthesis cannot prove the negative for later scholarship, so the flag is retained rather than upgraded.

audits.claim: KT S9 connects Heaven's authorization and the speaker's possession of qut with accession.
audits.retrieval_status: Retrieved full OA article PDF (16 pp.) from the journal site, converted with pdftotext and read; printed pagination present in page headers.
audits.source_locator: F. Verri, 'Törü, Kut and El in the Old Turkic political worldview: a contextual reconstruction and a symmetric comparison with the organization of Turkic states', Turkic Studies Journal 8(3) 2026, 83-98, DOI 10.32523/2664-5157-2026-3-83-98; KT S9 discussion on p.90.
audits.source_excerpt: At KT S9 the ruler states: teŋri yarlıkadukın üçün özüm kutum bar üçün qağan olurtum – in a cautious rendering, 'because Heaven favoured [me], and because I myself had kut, I became qaghan'. (32 words)
audits.basis: Direct retrieved quotation of the S9 formula containing both Heaven's favour (teŋri yarlıkadukın üçün) and possessed qut (özüm kutum bar üçün) with accession (qağan olurtum). The article also states the KT/BK face-line locator convention the entry's anchor list uses, and warns that 'grammar alone does not decide whether the concept is substance, fortune, capacity or authorisation', consistent with the entry's political-gloss calibration. Coupling tested: inscriptional wording to legitimation language, not an isolated bibliography fact.
audits.access_limit: None (OA journal PDF, retrieved in full). A 2026 article is fresh evidence rather than settled consensus; it is independently corroborated by Thomsen (1896) in TURK-03.

audits.claim: KT E31 compares the ruler's mother, a qatun, to Umay, and attaches qut to her (qut is not exclusively a male sovereign's term).
audits.retrieval_status: Same retrieved OCR text as TURK-03; located the I E31 translation, note, and transliteration blocks by local search.
audits.source_locator: Thomsen (1896), French translation of I E31 ('Par bonheur pour ma mère la katoun...'), note 37 to I E30-31 (Oumaï gloss via Radloff), and the transliteration fragment 'um*jl*^g ôgîm q^tun qutyfia'.
audits.source_excerpt: Par bonheur pour ma mère la katoun, qui ressemblait à (la déesse?) Oumaï, mon frère Kul-téghin lui tint lieu [de mari]. (24 words)
audits.basis: Thomsen renders E31 with the mother the qatun compared to Umay and with qut in the third-person possessive qutïŋa ('to/for her qut') attached to 'ögim qatun' (OCR fragment 'ôgîm q^tun qutyfia'; French 'Par bonheur pour ma mère la katoun'). This supports both the entry's Umay comparison and its statement that qut at E31 is attributed to the ruler's mother. Thomsen hedges the goddess reading ('(la déesse?)') and glosses Oumaï via Radloff's Shor material (protective spirit of children), consistent with the entry treating maternal protection as grounded while a complete Umay biography is not. Coupling tested: kinship/maternal authority to sacral vocabulary within one inscription line.
audits.access_limit: 1896 French translation via OCR; Tekin (1968)'s text for E31 not retrieved (lending-restricted). The 'childbirth/placenta' half of the entry's Umay row was not checked at Clauson level.

audits.claim: Ashina wolf-ancestry narratives are reported in Chinese histories (mutilated surviving boy, she-wolf, mountain refuge/cavern, sons from whom lineages arise) with variants across witnesses.
audits.retrieval_status: Retrieved full OA repository PDF, converted with pdftotext; printed page headers pp.125-136 intact across 19 PDF pages.
audits.source_locator: É. Kincses-Nagy, 'The Islamization of the Legend of the Turks: The Case of Oghuznāma', in Competing Narratives between Nomadic People and their Sedentary Neighbours (Studia Uralo-Altaica 53), 2019, 125-136; Ashina/Zhoushu passage with n.15 quoting Sinor 1982:224-225 on printed p.132.
audits.source_excerpt: the wolf took refuge and later gave birth to ten boys. The ten boys grew up and took wives from the outside. Each of the descendants took a surname and called himself A-shih-na (33 words)
audits.basis: The retrieved page attributes the story to the Zhoushu (completed around 629), notes the Beishi and Sui annals as slightly different versions, and identifies the ten sons as the later Ashina clan — matching the entry's narrative and its 'do not silently combine the witnesses' caution. The same article keeps the Oghuz grey (male) guide-wolf distinct from the Zhoushu she-wolf ancestress, supporting the entry's line 82 warning not to conflate the two narrative functions. Coupling tested: ancestry myth against transmitted/mediated history.
audits.access_limit: None for this article (OA). It quotes Sinor's English translation; Sinor 1982 itself and the underlying Chinese texts were not retrieved.

audits.claim: Distinguish Ashina (dynastic/clan designation) from modern retellings naming a she-wolf 'Asena'; an ancient witness for that personal name must be produced (to-verify).
audits.retrieval_status: Fetch blocked: SAGE returned HTTP 403 (no article text retrieved). Supplementary sweep: full-text search of the retrieved Kincses-Nagy (2019) article (620 text lines including bibliography) — 0 occurrences of 'Asena'.
audits.source_locator: Golden (2018), 'The Ethnogonic Tales of the Türks', The Medieval History Journal 21(2):291-327 — not retrievable; no passage locator available.
audits.source_excerpt: (no source text retrieved — HTTP 403; no excerpt available)
audits.basis: No retrievable source either attests an ancient personal name 'Asena' or documents its modern origin. The negative sweep is consistency evidence only: Kincses-Nagy (2019), an article devoted to these traditions, never uses the name, and the Sinor translation it quotes leaves the wolf unnamed while naming the clan A-shih-na. A tertiary pointer (Wikipedia 'Asena', retrieved) says the ancestress is 'mentioned, yet unnamed' citing Golden 2018, but Wikipedia is not full-text confirmation of Golden. The (to-verify) flag therefore stands; no erratum was appended and no verification-by-absence was recorded.
audits.access_limit: Golden 2018 paywalled (HTTP 403); no institutional access in this environment; Chinese primary texts not consulted.

audits.retrieval_status: Primary text NOT retrieved: the archive.org scan is lending-restricted — djvu.txt download HTTP 401, fulltext search-inside endpoint HTTP 403 anonymous, Google Books route HTTP 404. Only a secondary OA citation was retrieved (dergipark article PDF, full text).

audits.source_excerpt: Clauson,1971, s. 594 — 'سعادت و خوشبختی' (welfare and happiness). (≈12 words)
